Put \(d=k+1\) and \(n_0=2d+2=2k+4\).  We first treat the graph on the \(n_0\) displayed vertices in \(\mathrm{def:attaining\mbox{-}family}\).  It has \(3d\) directed arrows.  Its supplied set \(T\) contains the \(2d\) arrows out of \(0\) and the arrow \(P_1\to h\), so
\[
 |T|=2d+1=n_0-1,
 \qquad
 D\setminus T=\{P_i\to h:2\leq i\leq d\},
 \qquad
 |D\setminus T|=d-1=k.
\]
Every nonroot vertex has exactly one incoming arrow in \(T\), and every vertex is reached from \(0\).  Thus \(T\) is a rooted spanning arborescence.  The directed order with \(0\) first, then all \(P_i,Q_i\), and then \(h\), is topological, and \(e^{\star}=P_1\to h\) is an arrow.  Hence \(\mathrm{def:graph\mbox{-}class}\) gives
\[
 (G^{\star}_{k,n_0},T,e^{\star})\in\mathcal G_{n_0,k}.
\tag{1}
\]

We construct a regular covariance fiber.  Choose \(h_i\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\) and \(b_i\in\mathbb Q\) such that \(b_i^2>4h_i\), put \(H_0=\operatorname{diag}(h_1,\ldots,h_d)\), and let \(H\) be a rational symmetric positive-definite matrix, sufficiently close to \(H_0\), whose diagonal remains \((h_1,\ldots,h_d)\).  The additional generic requirement on \(H\) used below is compatible with an arbitrarily small such perturbation.  In the vertex order \((0,P_1,\ldots,P_d,Q_1,\ldots,Q_d,h)\), prescribe
\[
 \Sigma^{\star}=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1&0&0&1\\
 0&H&H&0\\
 0&H&C_0I_d&b\\
 1&0&b^{\mathsf T}&M
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad b=(b_1,\ldots,b_d)^{\mathsf T}.
\tag{2}
\]
Choose the rational number \(C_0\) so that \(C_0I_d-H\succ0\).  The Schur complement of \(H\) in
\(
 \left(\begin{smallmatrix}H&H\\H&C_0I_d\end{smallmatrix}\right)
\)
is \(C_0I_d-H\), so the principal block indexed by \(P,Q\) is positive definite.  After adjoining the independent \(0\)-coordinate, choose the rational number \(M\) larger than the corresponding final Schur-complement threshold.  These two Schur-complement inequalities prove
\[
 \Sigma^{\star}\succ0.
\tag{3}
\]

Write
\[
 a_i=\lambda_{0P_i},\qquad c_i=\lambda_{0Q_i},\qquad
 z_i=\lambda_{P_i h},\qquad z=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)^{\mathsf T},
 \qquad x=-Hz.
\]
The missing pairs in this family are \(P_i\leftrightarrow Q_i\), \(P_i\leftrightarrow h\), and \(Q_i\leftrightarrow h\), for \(1\leq i\leq d\); all other pairs are allowed by \(B\).  Substitution of (2) into the residual formula \(F_{ij}\) gives, respectively,
\[
 0=-a_i-(Hz)_i,
 \qquad
 0=b_i-c_i-(Hz)_i,
 \qquad
 0=h_i+a_ic_i.
\tag{4}
\]
Because \(H\) is invertible, (4) is equivalent to
\[
 a_i=x_i,qquad c_i=x_i+b_i,qquad
 x_i^2+b_ix_i+h_i=0\quad(1\leq i\leq d),
 \qquad z=-H^{-1}x.
\tag{5}
\]
The discriminant of the \(i\)-th quadratic is \(b_i^2-4h_i>0\).  Thus each quadratic has exactly two distinct real roots and (5) has exactly \(2^d\) real solutions.  Under the invertible change from \(z\) to \(x\), elimination of the two linear groups in (4) shows that the residual Jacobian is nonsingular precisely when
\[
 \det(H)\prod_{i=1}^d(2x_i+b_i)\ne0.
\tag{6}
\]
Both factors in (6) are nonzero at every solution, because \(H\succ0\) and
\((2x_i+b_i)^2=b_i^2-4h_i>0\).  Hence all \(2^d\) points are reduced.
For each of them, defining \(\Omega=(I_{n_0}-\Lambda)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{\star}(I_{n_0}-\Lambda)\) makes the equations in (4) exactly the required missing-bidirected zeros.  Acyclicity makes \(I_{n_0}-\Lambda\) invertible, and (3) then gives \(\Omega\succ0\) by congruence.  Thus every displayed point is a support-valid real positive-definite source lift.

We now choose \(H\) so that the original coefficient \(z_1=\lambda_{e^{\star}}\) separates them.  At \(H=H_0\), two branches with different first quadratic roots have different values \(z_1=-x_1/h_1\).  If two branches have the same first root but vectors \(x\ne x'\), choose \(j>1\) with \(x_j\ne x'_j\) and set
\[
 H(s)=H_0+s(E_{1j}+E_{j1}).
\]
Differentiating \(-H(s)^{-1}x\) at \(s=0\) gives
\[
 \left.\frac{d}{ds}\bigl(z_1(x)-z_1(x')\bigr)\right|_{s=0}
 =\frac{x_j-x'_j}{h_1h_j}\ne0.
\tag{7}
\]
Consequently, for every pair of branches, equality of their \(z_1\)-values is a proper algebraic condition on the off-diagonal entries of \(H\).  There are finitely many pairs.  The complement of their union is dense in a Euclidean neighborhood of \(H_0\), and rational matrices are dense there.  We may therefore choose the rational \(H\) used in (2) to preserve positive definiteness and (6) while making all \(2^d\) values of \(z_1\) distinct.

It remains to transfer this regular specialized fiber to the generic source-prime fiber and to rule out additional generic branches.  Let \(A_i,C_i,Z\) denote the multihomogeneous degree markers for the blocks \((a_i)\), \((c_i)\), and \((z_1,\ldots,z_d)\), of respective sizes \(1,1,d\).  The residual for \(P_i,Q_i\) has block degrees bounded by \(A_i+C_i\); those for \(P_i,h\) and \(Q_i,h\) have block degrees bounded by \(A_i+Z\) and \(C_i+Z\).  Therefore the coefficient in \(\mathrm{lem:multihomogeneous\mbox{-}bezout\mbox{-}isolated\mbox{-}bound}\) is
\[
 \left[\left(\prod_{i=1}^d A_iC_i\right)Z^d\right]
 \prod_{i=1}^d(A_i+C_i)(A_i+Z)(C_i+Z)=2^d.
\tag{8}
\]
Indeed, for each \(i\), exactly two selections produce \(A_iC_iZ\): choose \(A_i,Z,C_i\), or choose \(C_i,A_i,Z\), from the three factors in their displayed order.  Thus every zero-dimensional generic fiber has at most \(2^d\) points counted with multiplicity.  This count is made on the original polynomial residual system and therefore neither inverts a directed-coordinate denominator nor discards a zero-over-zero solution.

For completeness, we prove dominance and the lower degree directly.  There are exactly \(3d\) missing-bidirected residuals and \(3d\) directed coefficients.  If \(N=n_0=2d+2\), then
\[
 |D|+|B|+|V|
 =3d+\left\{\binom N2-3d\right\}+N
 =\frac{N(N+1)}2.
\tag{9}
\]
By \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\), the incidence space is integral and has this source dimension.  At any of the \(2^d\) points above, replace the covariance coordinates by \(\Sigma^{\star}+\xi\) and seek a formal coefficient vector
\[
 v(\xi)=v_0+\sum_{r\geq1}v_r(\xi),
\]
where \(v=(a,c,z)\) and \(v_r\) is homogeneous of degree \(r\) in the independent covariance increments \(\xi\).  At degree \(r\), the residual equations have the form
\[
 J(v_0)v_r=-R_r\bigl(\xi,v_1,\ldots,v_{r-1}\bigr),
\tag{10}
\]
where \(J(v_0)\) is the residual Jacobian and the right side is already determined.  Equation (6) makes \(J(v_0)\) invertible, so (10) recursively determines a unique \(v_r\) at every order.  If a covariance polynomial vanished on the incidence image, substitution into any such formal section would give that polynomial evaluated at \(\Sigma^{\star}+\xi\) as the zero formal series.  Algebraic independence of the entries of \(\xi\) then forces the polynomial itself to be zero.  Hence \(P_G=(0)\), the covariance projection is dominant, and (9) makes \(L/K_G\) finite.

The \(2^d\) formal sections lie over the common embedded covariance field
\(
 K_G\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Frac}\mathbb C[[\xi]]
\)
and their \(z_1\)-series are distinct because their constant terms are distinct.  If the minimal polynomial of \(z_1\) over \(K_G\) had degree smaller than \(2^d\), its image in \(\operatorname{Frac}\mathbb C[[\xi]][t]\) would have more distinct roots than its degree, which is impossible over a field.  Therefore
\[
 [K_G(z_1):K_G]\geq2^d.
\tag{11}
\]
The multihomogeneous count (8) gives \([L:K_G]\leq2^d\), so (11) forces
\[
 [K_G(z_1):K_G]=[L:K_G]=2^d.
\tag{12}
\]
Equivalently, the original coefficient \(e^{\star}=P_1\to h\) separates every generic branch.  Since the extension has characteristic zero, its minimal polynomial is separable.  Clearing its coefficient denominators and removing the nonzero discriminant, the residual Jacobian determinant, and the relevant leading coefficients leaves a nonempty Zariski-open covariance set on which the \(2^d\) queried values remain distinct.

Now append one of the fully bidirected children \(w\) of \(0\) specified in \(\mathrm{def:attaining\mbox{-}family}\), put \(x_w=\lambda_{0w}\), and let \(z_w\) collect the new covariance row \((\sigma_{iw}:i\in V)\) and \(\sigma_{ww}\).  There is no new missing-bidirected residual involving \(w\).  For fixed old source coordinates and \(x_w\), the covariance congruence is a triangular polynomial change, with polynomial inverse, between the newly allowed disturbance coordinates and \(z_w\).  If \(L_0,K_0\) are the old fields, the new fields therefore satisfy
\[
 L_1=L_0(x_w,z_w),\qquad K_1=K_0(z_w),
\tag{13}
\]
and the entries of \(z_w\) are algebraically independent over \(L_0(x_w)\).  If \(u_1,\ldots,u_{2^d}\) is a \(K_0\)-basis of \(K_0(z_1)\), a relation
\(
 \sum_j r_j(z_w)u_j=0
\)
over \(K_0(z_w)\), after clearing denominators and comparing coefficients of the algebraically independent monomials in \(z_w\), would be a \(K_0\)-linear relation among the \(u_j\).  Thus all \(r_j\) vanish; the same basis spans after adjoining \(z_w\).  Consequently
\[
 [K_1(z_1):K_1]=[K_0(z_1):K_0]=2^d.
\tag{14}
\]
Iteration proves \(d_{e^{\star}}(G^{\star}_{k,n})=2^{k+1}\) for every \(n\geq2k+4\).

Finally, \(d=k+1\geq1\) and \(n-2\geq2d\), so
\(
 \binom{n-2}{2}\geq\binom{2d}{2}=d(2d-1)\geq d
\).
Thus \(\mathrm{thm:orientation\mbox{-}upper\mbox{-}bound}\) gives \(D_k(n)\leq2^{k+1}\) throughout this regime, whereas the constructed member gives the reverse inequality.  Hence
\[
 D_k(n)=2^{k+1}\qquad(n\geq2k+4),
\]
with the asserted nonempty open separation set.

For a finite simple graph \(H=(W,E_H)\) and a vector \(r=(r_v:v\in W)\) of nonnegative integers, define
\[
 c_H(r)=
 \left[\prod_{v\in W}X_v^{r_v}\right]
 \prod_{\{u,v\}\in E_H}(X_u+X_v).
\tag{15}
\]
Choosing \(X_v\) from the factor belonging to \(\{u,v\}\) is equivalent to orienting that edge toward \(v\).  Hence \(c_H(r)\) is exactly the number of orientations of \(H\) with indegree vector \(r\), and in particular
\[
 c_H(r)=0\quad\hbox{unless}\quad
 \sum_{v\in W}r_v=|E_H|,
 \qquad 0\leq r_v\leq\deg_H(v).
\tag{16}
\]

If \(|W|\leq2\), simplicity leaves at most one edge, whose direction is fixed by \(r\); thus \(c_H(r)\leq1\).  If \(|W|\leq3\) and \(H\) is a forest, two orientations with the same indegrees would have a nonempty balanced symmetric difference.  Following an entering edge by a leaving edge in that difference would produce a cycle, contradicting that \(H\) is a forest.  Thus the count is at most one.  The only remaining graph is a triangle.  Its two cyclic orientations both have indegree vector \((1,1,1)\), while each transitive orientation is uniquely determined by its labeled permutation of \((0,1,2)\).  Therefore
\[
 \max_{|W|\leq3,r}c_H(r)=2.
\tag{17}
\]

Suppose next that \(|W|\leq4\).  When \(|E_H|\leq4\), every component is a tree except possibly one unicyclic component: two independent cycles in a simple graph require either at least five edges on four vertices or more than four vertices.  Given an indegree vector, the direction of the edge at a leaf is forced; deleting leaves iteratively fixes every edge outside the unique cycle.  Two orientations of a cycle with the same residual indegrees can differ only on the entire cycle, giving at most its two cyclic orientations.  Componentwise,
\[
 c_H(r)\leq2\qquad(|W|\leq4, |E_H|\leq4).
\tag{18}
\]

With five edges the only possibility is \(H=K_4\setminus\{\{1,2\}\}\).  For
\[
 P=(X_1+X_3)(X_1+X_4)(X_2+X_3)(X_2+X_4)(X_3+X_4),
\]
choosing the number \(a\) of \(X_1\)-terms in the first two factors and the number \(b\) of \(X_2\)-terms in the next two factors, then collecting the two choices in the last factor, gives the exact coefficient maxima
\[
 \begin{array}{c|ccc}
  &b=0&b=1&b=2\\ \hline
 a=0&1&2&1\\
 a=1&2&3&2\\
 a=2&1&2&1.
 \end{array}
\tag{19}
\]
Thus every five-edge coefficient is at most three.  If all four block capacities are positive, (16) forces a permutation of \((2,1,1,1)\); (19) gives coefficient three when the exponent two is at vertex \(3\) or \(4\), and coefficient two when it is at vertex \(1\) or \(2\).

With six edges one has \(H=K_4\).  Up to sorting, the only exponent vectors satisfying (16) and \(0\leq r_v\leq3\) are
\[
 (0,0,3,3),\quad(0,1,2,3),\quad(0,2,2,2),
 \quad(1,1,1,3),\quad(1,1,2,2).
\tag{20}
\]
The first coefficient is zero because the edge joining the two zero-exponent vertices has no permissible endpoint.  A labeled vector of type \((0,1,2,3)\) forces the unique transitive orientation.  In types \((0,2,2,2)\) and \((1,1,1,3)\), the edges at the extreme vertex are forced and the remaining triangle has its two cyclic orientations.  For \(r=(1,1,2,2)\), condition on the factor \(X_1+X_2\).  If it contributes \(X_1\), the factors on edges \(13\) and \(14\) must contribute \(X_3X_4\), and the remaining triangle on \(2,3,4\) has two cyclic choices.  The choice \(X_2\) is symmetric.  Therefore
\[
 [X_1X_2X_3^2X_4^2]
 \prod_{1\leq i<j\leq4}(X_i+X_j)=2+2=4,
\tag{21}
\]
and (18)--(21) prove that four is the maximum on four blocks.

We connect these counts to the SEM system.  In the square subsystem used in \(\mathrm{thm:orientation\mbox{-}upper\mbox{-}bound}\), variables are partitioned by child vertex.  The root of \(T\) has a directed path in \(T\) to every other vertex; an additional arrow into that root would therefore create a directed cycle and is excluded by acyclicity.  Thus the root block is empty and there are at most \(n-1\) nonempty child blocks.  The displayed formula for \(F_{ij}\) has degree at most one in the block for child \(i\), at most one in the block for child \(j\), and zero in every other child block.  An unordered pair \(\{i,j\}\) supplies at most the one residual \(F_{ij}\); hence the binary-factor graph is simple.  By \(\mathrm{lem:multihomogeneous\mbox{-}bezout\mbox{-}isolated\mbox{-}bound}\), its prescribed multidegree coefficient is the orientation count (15).  Equations (17) and (21), together with the two-block argument, yield
\[
 d_e(G)\leq1\quad(n=3),\qquad
 d_e(G)\leq2\quad(n=4),\qquad
 d_e(G)\leq4\quad(n=5)
\tag{22}
\]
whenever the queried coordinate is algebraic.

Finally suppose \(n=5\) and \(|D\setminus T|\leq1\).  Then \(|D|\leq4+1=5\), so a selected square subsystem has at most five equations and, after its unary factors are removed, at most five binary factors.  Four or fewer binary factors are covered by (18) and give coefficient at most two.  Five binary factors force four nonempty blocks and the graph \(K_4\setminus e\); there is then no unary factor, the four positive block sizes sum to five, and hence their capacity vector is a permutation of \((2,1,1,1)\).  Equation (19) bounds its coefficient by three.  Therefore
\[
 d_e(G)\leq3\qquad(n=5, |D\setminus T|\leq1),
\tag{23}
\]
which proves every assertion.

The displayed \(T\) has four arrows, gives each nonroot vertex exactly one parent, and contains a directed path from \(0\) to every vertex.  It is therefore a rooted spanning arborescence.  Moreover,
\[
 D\setminus T=\{2\to3,2\to4\},
\]
the order \(0<1<2<3<4\) is topological for \(D\), and \(e=2\to4\) belongs to \(D\).  By \(\mathrm{def:graph\mbox{-}class}\),
\[
 (G^{(4)},T,e)\in\mathcal G_{5,2}.
\tag{24}
\]

Put
\[
 (a,b,c,d,u,f)=
 (\lambda_{01},\lambda_{02},\lambda_{13},
   \lambda_{23},\lambda_{14},\lambda_{24}).
\]
At the rational source point
\[
 (a,b,c,d,u,f)=(2,3,4,5,6,7),
 \qquad
 \Omega^{\star}=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 30&1&2&3&4\\
 1&31&0&0&0\\
 2&0&32&0&0\\
 3&0&0&33&0\\
 4&0&0&0&34
 \end{pmatrix},
\tag{25}
\]
the only nonzero off-diagonal disturbance entries are allowed by \(B\).  For every nonzero \(y\in\mathbb R^5\), applying \(2|y_iy_j|\leq y_i^2+y_j^2\) to the four off-diagonal terms gives
\[
 y^{\mathsf T}\Omega^{\star}y
 \geq20y_0^2+30y_1^2+30y_2^2+30y_3^2+30y_4^2>0.
\tag{26}
\]
Thus \(\Omega^{\star}\succ0\).  Direct multiplication in the covariance parametrization yields
\[
 \Sigma^{\star}=
 (I_5-\Lambda^{\star})^{-\mathsf T}
 \Omega^{\star}(I_5-\Lambda^{\star})^{-1}
 =\begin{pmatrix}
 30&61&92&707&1014\\
 61&155&187&1561&2247\\
 92&187&314&2327&3332\\
 707&1561&2327&17981&25747\\
 1014&2247&3332&25747&36972
 \end{pmatrix}.
\tag{27}
\]
Since \(I_5-\Lambda^{\star}\) is unit triangular in the displayed topological order, it is invertible; (26) and congruence also give \(\Sigma^{\star}\succ0\).

The missing bidirected pairs are the six pairs among \(\{1,2,3,4\}\).  Substitution of (27) into their residuals gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 r_{12}&=30ab-92a-61b+187,\\
 r_{13}&=61ac+92ad-707a-155c-187d+1561,\\
 r_{14}&=61au+92af-1014a-155u-187f+2247,\\
 r_{23}&=61bc+92bd-707b-187c-314d+2327,\\
 r_{24}&=61bu+92bf-1014b-187u-314f+3332,\\
 r_{34}&=155cu+187cf-2247c+187du+314df-3332d\\
 &\hspace{2.8em}{}-1561u-2327f+25747.
\end{aligned}
\tag{28}
\]
Exact polynomial arithmetic over \(\mathbb Q\) gives the following triangular generating set for the same ideal \(J^{\star}=(r_{12},r_{13},r_{14},r_{23},r_{24},r_{34})\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
 g_a={}&384915840a+425450175590061f^3-8965411803407607f^2\\
 &{}+62974399432228195f-147445028655847225,\\
 g_b={}&741827520b-593375419233f^3+12321625507347f^2\\
 &{}-85271405126447f+196665729339485,\\
 g_c={}&615040c+25798931271f^3-543666188277f^2\\
 &{}+3818873142057f-8941504654939,\\
 g_d={}&4d-3f+1,\\
 g_u={}&153760u+8599643757f^3-181222062759f^2\\
 &{}+1272957714019f-2980501654153,\\
 g_f={}&8599643757f^4-241347527724f^3+2539994011474f^2\\
 &{}-11880540850068f+20838536737025.
\end{aligned}
\tag{29}
\]
This equality of ideals is an exact two-sided certificate: division of every polynomial in (28) by the list (29) has zero remainder, and reverse exact division expresses every polynomial in (29) as a polynomial combination over \(\mathbb Q\) of the six polynomials in (28).  Thus both ideal inclusions are finite rational identities; no numerical root calculation is being used.

The last polynomial factors as
\[
 g_f=q(f)=(f-7)c(f),
\]
where
\[
 c(f)=8599643757f^3-181150021425f^2
      +1271943861499f-2976933819575.
\tag{30}
\]
Exact integer arithmetic gives
\[
 c(7)=-30256,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{disc}(c)
 =1802165059445823134111101206528>0.
\tag{31}
\]
To derive the real-root conclusion, if a real cubic with leading coefficient \(A\) has roots \(r_1,r_2,r_3\), then its discriminant is
\[
 A^4\prod_{i<j}(r_i-r_j)^2.
\]
If only one root \(r\) were real, the others would be \(s+it\) and \(s-it\), with \(t\ne0\), and the product would equal
\[
 -4A^4t^2\bigl((r-s)^2+t^2\bigr)^2<0.
\]
The positive discriminant in (31) therefore gives three distinct real roots of \(c\), and \(c(7)\ne0\) excludes \(7\).  Hence \(q\) has four distinct real roots.

All five leading coefficients of \(g_a,g_b,g_c,g_d,g_u\) in their respective non-\(f\) variables are nonzero rational integers.  Each root of \(q\) consequently gives exactly one real value of each of \(a,b,c,d,u\), and the ideal equality above gives
\[
 \mathbb C[a,b,c,d,u,f]/J^{\star}
 \cong\mathbb C[f]/(q)
 \cong\mathbb C^4.
\tag{32}
\]
Thus the specialized residual fiber consists of exactly four reduced points with distinct real \(f\)-coordinates.  The root \(f=7\) recovers the source point (25), so the fiber is nonempty.

We next pass to the generic coordinate degree.  The Jacobian of the triangular generators (29) is nonsingular at every point of (32): its five non-\(f\) diagonal entries are the displayed nonzero constants and its remaining diagonal entry is \(q'(f)\ne0\).  Differentiating the polynomial identities establishing the two ideal inclusions shows that the row spans of the differentials of (28) and (29) agree at their common zeros.  Hence the residual Jacobian of (28) has rank six at all four points.

Write the fifteen covariance coordinates as \(s=\Sigma^{\star}+z\) and the residual map as \(R(s,v)\), where \(v=(a,b,c,d,u,f)\).  At any of the four points \(v_0\), seek
\[
 v(z)=v_0+\sum_{r\geq1}v_r(z),
\]
with \(v_r\) homogeneous of degree \(r\) in \(z\).  At degree \(r\), the equation is
\[
 \left.\frac{\partial R}{\partial v}\right|_{(\Sigma^{\star},v_0)}v_r
 =-H_r(v_1,\ldots,v_{r-1};z).
\tag{33}
\]
The invertible residual Jacobian determines exactly one \(v_r\) at every step, so all four points lift to formal branches over \(\mathbb C[[z]]\), with distinct \(f\)-series because their constant terms differ.

By \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\), the incidence space is integral.  Here the source dimension is
\[
 |D|+|B|+|V|=6+4+5=15,
\tag{34}
\]
which equals the dimension of the symmetric covariance space.  If a covariance polynomial vanished on the incidence image, substituting any section (33) would make its value at \(\Sigma^{\star}+z\) the zero formal series.  Algebraic independence of the covariance increments forces that polynomial to be zero.  Therefore \(P_G=(0)\), \(K_G=\mathbb C(s)\), and (34) makes \(L/K_G\) a finite extension.

For its upper degree, partition the six directed variables into the four child blocks
\[
 A=(a),\qquad B_0=(b),\qquad C=(c,d),\qquad U_0=(u,f),
\]
of sizes \((1,1,2,2)\).  The six residuals are indexed by the six pairs of distinct blocks and have degree at most one in each incident block.  Thus \(\mathrm{lem:multihomogeneous\mbox{-}bezout\mbox{-}isolated\mbox{-}bound}\) and \(\mathrm{lem:small\mbox{-}block\mbox{-}orientation\mbox{-}maxima}\) give
\[
 [L:K_G]\leq
 [A B_0 C^2U_0^2]
 (A+B_0)(A+C)(A+U_0)(B_0+C)(B_0+U_0)(C+U_0)=4.
\tag{35}
\]
The four formal branches in (33) give the reverse inequality: any polynomial over the embedded field \(K_G\subset\operatorname{Frac}\mathbb C[[z]]\) has at most its degree many distinct roots, whereas the four \(f\)-series are distinct.  Hence
\[
 [L:K_G]=[K_G(f):K_G]=4,
 \qquad d_{,2\to4}(G^{(4)})=4.
\tag{36}
\]
The exact localization in \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\) inverts no directed-coordinate expression, so (36) is the source-prime generic queried-coordinate degree and retains all finite values.

Every specialized root also has the claimed supported positive-definite real lift.  The linear equations in (29) recover a real acyclic matrix \(\widetilde\Lambda\) from each real root of \(q\).  Define
\[
 \widetilde\Omega=(I_5-\widetilde\Lambda)^{\mathsf T}
 \Sigma^{\star}(I_5-\widetilde\Lambda).
\tag{37}
\]
Equations (28) are exactly the six entries of (37) required to vanish, so \(\widetilde\Omega_{ij}=0\) whenever \(i\leftrightarrow j\notin B\).  Acyclicity makes \(I_5-\widetilde\Lambda\) unit triangular and invertible.  Since \(\Sigma^{\star}\succ0\), congruence in (37) gives \(\widetilde\Omega\succ0\).  Thus all four real roots, and not merely the original one, have real support-valid positive-definite lifts; this statement does not assert real uniqueness.

Finally append a vertex \(w\) with sole directed edge \(0\to w\), put this edge in \(T\), and allow every bidirected pair incident with \(w\).  The enlarged \(T\) is still a rooted spanning arborescence, the directed support remains acyclic, and the number of excess arrows remains two.  No new missing-bidirected residual is introduced.  Let \(L_0,K_0\) denote the old source and covariance fields, let \(x=\lambda_{0w}\), and let \(z_w\) consist of the new covariance row and diagonal.  For fixed old source coordinates and \(x\), covariance congruence gives a triangular polynomial bijection, with polynomial inverse, between the newly allowed disturbance coordinates and \(z_w\).  Hence
\[
 L_1=L_0(x,z_w),\qquad K_1=K_0(z_w),
\tag{38}
\]
where \(x\) and the entries of \(z_w\) are algebraically independent over \(L_0\).  If \(w_1,\ldots,w_4\) is a \(K_0\)-basis of \(K_0(f)\), clearing denominators in a relation over \(K_0(z_w)\) and comparing coefficients of the algebraically independent monomials in \(z_w\) proves that the same elements remain independent; they also span because powers of \(f\) reduce in the old basis.  Therefore
\[
 [K_1(f):K_1]=[K_0(f):K_0]=4.
\tag{39}
\]
Iteration proves the appending assertion.  At five vertices, \(\mathcal G_{5,2}\subseteq\mathcal G_{5,k}\) for every admissible \(k\geq2\), so (36) gives \(D_k(5)\geq4\).

The admissible range is \(0\leq k\leq(n-1)(n-2)/2\).  When \(n=2\), it forces \(k=0\), and \(\mathrm{lem:tree\mbox{-}maxima\mbox{-}support}\) gives
\[
 D_0(2)=1.
\]

When \(n=3\), one has \(k\in\{0,1\}\).  The two-block conclusion of \(\mathrm{lem:small\mbox{-}block\mbox{-}orientation\mbox{-}maxima}\) gives \(d_e(G)\leq1\) for every finite query in either class.  Because a graph with zero excess also satisfies every larger admissible budget,
\[
 \mathcal G_{3,0}\subseteq\mathcal G_{3,k}.
\tag{40}
\]
The tree witness \(D_0(3)=1\) in \(\mathrm{lem:tree\mbox{-}maxima\mbox{-}support}\), together with (40), supplies the reverse inequality.  Hence
\[
 D_k(3)=1\qquad(0\leq k\leq1).
\tag{41}
\]

When \(n=4\), the three-block bound gives \(d_e(G)\leq2\) for every finite query and every admissible \(k\).  The inclusion \(\mathcal G_{4,0}\subseteq\mathcal G_{4,k}\) and the separating degree-two tree witness in \(\mathrm{lem:tree\mbox{-}maxima\mbox{-}support}\) give \(D_k(4)\geq2\).  Therefore
\[
 D_k(4)=2\qquad(0\leq k\leq3).
\tag{42}
\]

For \(n=5,k=0\), the same tree lemma gives \(D_0(5)=2\).  For \(k=1\), equation (23) gives \(D_1(5)\leq3\), while \(\mathrm{lem:five\mbox{-}node\mbox{-}cubic\mbox{-}coordinate\mbox{-}transfer}\) supplies a member of \(\mathcal G_{5,1}\) and an original edge of degree three.  Thus
\[
 D_1(5)=3.
\tag{43}
\]
For every admissible \(k\geq2\), the four-block bound gives \(D_k(5)\leq4\).  The proved quartic witness belongs to \(\mathcal G_{5,2}\), and budget monotonicity gives \(\mathcal G_{5,2}\subseteq\mathcal G_{5,k}\); hence \(D_k(5)\geq4\).  Consequently
\[
 D_k(5)=4\qquad(2\leq k\leq6).
\tag{44}
\]
Equations (41)--(44), with the two-vertex conclusion, give the displayed table.  The cited tree constructions, the cubic coordinate transfer, and the quartic witness each use an original directed coefficient.  Their degrees equal the number of distinct generic conjugate values; in characteristic zero the relevant minimal polynomials are separable.  Thus those coefficients separate the asserted generic branches.

Fix an admissible \(k\) and \(n\geq4\), and put
\[
 j=\min\{k,\lfloor(n-4)/2\rfloor\}.
\tag{45}
\]
Then \(0\leq j\leq k\) and \(n\geq2j+4\).  Applying \(\mathrm{thm:large\mbox{-}size\mbox{-}frontier}\) with excess budget \(j\) gives a one-sink graph-query in \(\mathcal G_{n,j}\) whose original edge satisfies
\[
 d_{e^{\star}}(G^{\star}_{j,n})=2^{j+1}.
\tag{46}
\]
By \(\mathrm{def:graph\mbox{-}class}\), every graph with at most \(j\) excess arrows also has at most \(k\) excess arrows, so
\[
 \mathcal G_{n,j}\subseteq\mathcal G_{n,k}.
\tag{47}
\]
Taking the maximum defining \(D_k(n)\) and using (46)--(47) yields
\[
 D_k(n)\geq2^{j+1}.
\tag{48}
\]
For every integer \(n\geq4\),
\[
 \lfloor(n-4)/2\rfloor+1=\lfloor(n-2)/2\rfloor,
\]
and for nonnegative integers \(k\) and \(a\), \(\min\{k,a\}+1=\min\{k+1,a+1\}\).  Therefore (45) gives
\[
 j+1=\min\{k+1,\lfloor(n-2)/2\rfloor\}.
\tag{49}
\]
Substitution of (49) into (48) proves
\[
 D_k(n)\geq2^{\min\{k+1,\lfloor(n-2)/2\rfloor\}}.
\]
The construction in (46) uses the original coefficient \(e^{\star}\), as required.  The separate sharper statements at \(n=5\), namely \(D_1(5)=3\) and \(D_k(5)=4\) for \(k\geq2\), follow directly from \(\mathrm{thm:small\mbox{-}size\mbox{-}frontier}\); they are stated separately because the one-sink envelope need not be sharp there.

proposed.statement:
For every \(k\ge0\) and \(n\ge2k+4\), \(d_{e^{\star}}(G^{\star}_{k,n})=2^{k+1}\) and therefore
\[
D_k(n)=2^{k+1}.
\]
One original coefficient \(e^{\star}\) separates all branches on a nonempty Zariski-open covariance set.
proposed.justification: A uniform attaining region turns the exponent from a loose Bezout count into a sharp coordinate frontier for a substantial size range.
proposed.gap: Foygel, Draisma, and Drton already exhibit cubic and quartic behavior in small SEMs, but not an all-\(k\) family with one edge separating \(2^{k+1}\) generic branches.
proposed.consumer: Software maintainers obtain adversarial benchmark families and users obtain a worst-case ambiguity warning indexed by the number of added parents.

proofs.proof_tex:
Condition on the successful symbolic event of \(\mathrm{thm:conditional\mbox{-}geometric\mbox{-}resolution}\).  That theorem and the Schwartz--Zippel allocation in its proof give this event probability at least \(1-\delta\).  Each circuit retained in \(\mathcal Q_{G,e}\) has a nonzero pullback under the covariance parametrization.  Its class in the domain \(R_G\cong\operatorname{im}\phi_G\) is therefore nonzero.  The finite product of these classes is nonzero, so the cleared product \(h_{G,e}\) is not the zero polynomial on the model image.  Hence
\[
 \mathcal E_{G,e}=V(h_{G,e})                                \tag{9}
\]
is a proper algebraic subset of that image.

The equality \(p_e(\lambda_e)=0\) holds in the integral generic-fiber algebra \(A_K\).  Clearing only covariance denominators gives some \(a\in S_G\) and incidence polynomials \(c_{ij}\) such that
\[
 a(\Sigma)p_e(\Sigma,\lambda_e)
 =\sum_{\substack{i\ne j\\ i\leftrightarrow j\notin B}}
 c_{ij}(\Sigma,\Lambda)F_{ij}(\Lambda,\Sigma).              \tag{10}
\]
The cleared factor \(a\) is among the covariance-localization circuits in \(\mathcal Q_{G,e}\).  Therefore, if \(h_{G,e}(\Sigma)\ne0\), every specialized solution of all original residual equations satisfies \(p_e(\Sigma,\lambda_e)=0\).  By the definition of \(\mathcal Z_e\), (10) proves
\[
 \mathcal Z_e(G,\Sigma)
 \subseteq \{z\in\mathbb C:p_e(\Sigma,z)=0\}.               \tag{11}
\]

For the converse, put \(E=K_G(\lambda_e)\).  For every \(K_G\)-embedding \(\tau:E\to\overline{K_G}\), the tensor product \(L\otimes_{E,\tau}\overline{K_G}\) is nonzero.  Choosing an \(E\)-transcendence basis gives a dominant rational map from the corresponding conjugate component to an affine space of the same dimension.  There are only \(d_e(G)\) such components, so the intersection of their nonempty generic slicing loci is nonempty.  The coordinate-preserving slice constructed in the conditional geometric-resolution theorem consequently meets every conjugate branch and is zero-dimensional.  By \(\mathrm{lem:generic\mbox{-}rur\mbox{-}specialization}\), its rational univariate representation specializes with its finite points and multiplicities preserved away from the loci where dimension, a denominator, a leading coefficient, a point at infinity, or separation degenerates.  Every such locus is represented by a factor of \(h_{G,e}\).  The returned lifting identities, again among the factors certified in \(\mathcal Q_{G,e}\), verify by substitution that every specialized RUR point satisfies every original \(F_{ij}\).  Hence every root of \(p_e(\Sigma,\cdot)\) has a lift to the original incidence scheme, and
\[
 \{z\in\mathbb C:p_e(\Sigma,z)=0\}
 \subseteq\mathcal Z_e(G,\Sigma).                            \tag{12}
\]
This argument slices only to construct the certificate; it lifts back to \(I_G\), so it remains valid when the unsliced \(\Lambda\)-fiber is positive dimensional.

Equations (11)--(12) prove the asserted equality.  The pole and incidence-lifting factors retain components on which an intermediate formula has a pole or is identically zero-over-zero.  The homogenized leading-form and specialized-leading-coefficient factors prevent a finite point from being exchanged with a projective-infinity point or lost through a degree drop.  Finally, characteristic zero makes the minimal polynomial \(p_e\) separable over \(K_G\); outside the squarefreeness-resultant factor in \(h_{G,e}\), its specialization remains squarefree.  Thus all displayed roots are distinct there, completing the proof on an event of probability at least \(1-\delta\).

Fix \(G=(V,D,B)\).  Write \(s=(s_{ij}:i\leq j)\) for real symmetric covariance indeterminates, \(z\) for the queried value, and \(\ell=(\ell_f:f\in D)\) for real directed-coefficient indeterminates.  Define the ordered-field formula
\[
 \Phi_G(s,z)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
 \exists\ell\in\mathbb R^D\left[
   \ell_e=z\ \wedge
   \bigwedge_{\substack{i\ne j\\i\leftrightarrow j\notin B}}
      F_{ij}(\ell,s)=0
 \right].                                                     \tag{13}
\]
All polynomials in (13) have rational coefficients, because each residual uses only addition and multiplication with coefficients \(0,1,-1\), while \(D\) and \(B\) only select variables and equations.  The definition of the retained real set gives, for every real symmetric \(\Sigma\) and real \(z\),
\[
 \Phi_G(\Sigma,z)
 \Longleftrightarrow z\in\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma).             \tag{14}
\]

Apply \(\mathrm{lem:effective\mbox{-}real\mbox{-}quantifier\mbox{-}elimination}\) to (13), with \(\ell\) quantified and \((s,z)\) free.  It produces an effectively computable formula
\[
 \Psi_G(s,z)=
 \bigvee_a\bigwedge_b
 \bigl(\operatorname{sign}g_{ab}(s,z)=\epsilon_{ab}\bigr),
 \qquad g_{ab}\in\mathbb Q[s,z],\quad
 \epsilon_{ab}\in\{-1,0,1\},                               \tag{15}
\]
equivalent to \(\Phi_G\) over every real closed field.  Combining (14) and (15) gives the required computable if-and-only-if characterization.  Because (13) uses the original residual equations without division or a zero-dimensionality restriction, this characterization also covers positive-dimensional fibers and components contained in a denominator-zero locus of an intermediate reduction.

Now impose the theorem's chart and successful-output antecedents.  If \(\Sigma\succ0\) is in the real covariance-model image and outside \(\mathcal E_{G,e}\), then \(\mathrm{thm:exceptional\mbox{-}set\mbox{-}validity}\) gives
\[
 \{z\in\mathbb C:p_e(\Sigma,z)=0\}
 =\mathcal Z_e(G,\Sigma).                                    \tag{16}
\]
The squarefreeness factor in \(h_{G,e}\) is nonzero at \(\Sigma\), so all roots in (16) are simple.  Formula (15) then decides independently, for each real root, whether it has a complete real supported extension.  In particular, neither complex degree nor local rank is used as a real-uniqueness assertion.

Suppose the entries of \(\Sigma\) are supplied by exact real-algebraic univariate representations and isolating data.  Every coefficient circuit of \(p_e\) can then be evaluated exactly because all its certified denominators are nonzero.  Clear a known nonzero common denominator.  Applying \(\mathrm{lem:real\mbox{-}algebraic\mbox{-}sampling}\) to the resulting univariate equation produces a point on every connected component of its real zero set.  Squarefreeness makes that set finite, so these components are exactly the individual real roots.  Exact sign determination orders the roots and removes duplicate encodings, and rational sign bisection terminates with disjoint isolating intervals because the roots are distinct.

For an enumerated real root \(z\), exact sign determination evaluates every atom of (15).  If \(\Psi_G(\Sigma,z)\) is false, the root representation, isolating interval, and sign vector are a finite rejecting record.  If it is true, define
\[
 Q_{\Sigma,z}(\ell)
 = (\ell_e-z)^2+
 \sum_{\substack{i\ne j\\i\leftrightarrow j\notin B}}
 F_{ij}(\ell,\Sigma)^2.                                      \tag{17}
\]
Over an ordered field a sum of squares is zero exactly when every summand is zero.  Thus
\[
 Z_{\mathbb R}(Q_{\Sigma,z})\ne\varnothing
 \Longleftrightarrow \Phi_G(\Sigma,z)
 \Longleftrightarrow z\in\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma).             \tag{18}
\]
In the accepting case, the real-algebraic-sampling lemma applied to (17), over the ordered coefficient domain generated by \(\Sigma\) and \(z\), returns a real univariate representation of a point on every semialgebraically connected component of its zero set.  Selecting any returned point gives a complete lift \(\ell\) with \(\ell_e=z\) satisfying every original residual.  Conversely, any point recorded by an accepting certificate makes every summand in (17) vanish.  The root representation and interval, the exact sign vector in (15), and, in the accepting case, this lift representation constitute the finite \(\mathsf{LiftCert}\), which accepts exactly the roots in \(\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma)\).  A finite tower of real algebraic coefficient extensions can be encoded by one primitive real algebraic element: for algebraic \(a,b\), only finitely many rational \(c\) fail to separate the conjugate pairs of \(a+cb\); iterating this observation reduces the tower to a single univariate representation, and an isolating interval selects the intended real embedding.

It remains to verify support and positivity.  Let \(\Lambda\in\mathbb R^D\) be an accepted lift and put \(R=I_n-\Lambda\).  Acyclicity supplies a topological order in which \(\Lambda\) is strictly triangular, hence nilpotent; therefore \(R\) is invertible.  Set
\[
 \Omega=R^{\mathsf T}\Sigma R.                               \tag{19}
\]
For every nonzero real vector \(x\), one has \(Rx\ne0\), and positive definiteness of \(\Sigma\) gives
\[
 x^{\mathsf T}\Omega x=(Rx)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(Rx)>0.        \tag{20}
\]
Thus \(\Omega\succ0\).  Entrywise expansion of (19) yields
\[
 \Omega_{ij}
 =\sigma_{ij}
 -\sum_{p\in\operatorname{pa}_D(i)}\lambda_{pi}\sigma_{pj}
 -\sum_{q\in\operatorname{pa}_D(j)}\lambda_{qj}\sigma_{iq}
 +\sum_{p\in\operatorname{pa}_D(i)}
       \sum_{q\in\operatorname{pa}_D(j)}
       \lambda_{pi}\lambda_{qj}\sigma_{pq}
 =F_{ij}(\Lambda,\Sigma).                                    \tag{21}
\]
The accepting residual equations make (21) zero whenever \(i\leftrightarrow j\notin B\), exactly the noise-support restriction.  Finally, (19) and invertibility of \(R\) imply \(\Sigma=R^{-\mathsf T}\Omega R^{-1}\).  Hence every accepted root, and only such a root, extends to a real supported SEM, with positive-definite recovered disturbance covariance.

Work under the valid-chart and successful-output antecedents.  On this event, \(\mathrm{thm:exceptional\mbox{-}set\mbox{-}validity}\) says that \(h_{G,e}\) is nonzero in the covariance-model coordinate ring.  Put
\[
 N=|D|+|B|+n
\]
and identify the free real entries of \((\Lambda,\Omega)\), subject only to the prescribed support, with \(\mathbb R^N\).  The set
\[
 \mathcal S_+
 =\{(\Lambda,\Omega)\in\mathbb R^N:\Omega\succ0\}           \tag{22}
\]
is nonempty because it contains \((0,I_n)\), and is Euclidean open in this support space because strict positive definiteness is stable under sufficiently small perturbations.

The set \(\mathcal S_+\) is Zariski dense in the corresponding complex source space.  Indeed, it contains a real open box about \((0,I_n)\).  If a complex polynomial vanishes on that box, fix all but one coordinate; the resulting univariate polynomial has infinitely many roots and is zero.  Repeating this argument coordinate by coordinate makes every coefficient zero.

For the fixed acyclic graph, define the source parametrization
\[
 \Phi_G(\Lambda,\Omega)
 =(I_n-\Lambda)^{-\mathsf T}\Omega(I_n-\Lambda)^{-1}.         \tag{23}
\]
In a topological order \(\Lambda^n=0\), so each inverse in (23) is the finite sum \(I_n+\Lambda+\cdots+\Lambda^{n-1}\); hence \(\Phi_G\) is polynomial.  Nonzeroness of \(h_{G,e}\) in \(R_G\) means that the source polynomial \(h_{G,e}\circ\Phi_G\) is nonzero.  Zariski density of (22) therefore supplies \((\Lambda_0,\Omega_0)\in\mathcal S_+\) such that
\[
 h_{G,e}(\Phi_G(\Lambda_0,\Omega_0))\ne0.                    \tag{24}
\]
With \(\Sigma_0=\Phi_G(\Lambda_0,\Omega_0)\), equation (24) gives
\[
 \Sigma_0\in\mathcal M_G\setminus\mathcal E_{G,e}.          \tag{25}
\]

The model image is semialgebraic: it is the projection of the source set described by the polynomial covariance equations, the linear missing-bidirected equalities, and the strict principal-minor inequalities for \(\Omega\succ0\); effective real quantifier elimination removes the source coordinates.  The exceptional complement and each sign condition in the real-lifting formula are semialgebraic as well.  Outside the leading-coefficient and squarefreeness factors in \(h_{G,e}\), the degree of \(p_e(\Sigma,\cdot)\) is fixed and every root is simple.  The assertion that \(z\) is the \(j\)-th real root is an ordered-field formula: it asserts \(p_e(\Sigma,z)=0\) and the existence of exactly \(j-1\) distinct real roots below \(z\).  Clearing the certified nonzero denominators and applying quantifier elimination shows that each ordered-root graph is semialgebraic.  Intersecting it with the real-lifting sign formula and projecting to covariance space shows that the locus on which that ordered root is extendable is also semialgebraic.

Apply \(\mathrm{lem:semialgebraic\mbox{-}stratification}\) to the finite common refinement by the model image, the exceptional complement, the possible real-root counts, and these extendability loci, and split the resulting smooth strata into connected components.  The component through \(\Sigma_0\) is a connected smooth semialgebraic cell
\[
 \mathcal C_{G,e}\subseteq
 \mathcal M_G\setminus\mathcal E_{G,e}                       \tag{26}
\]
on which the number of simple real roots and every ordered root's extension label are constant.  This is the cell required by \(\mathrm{def:regular\mbox{-}cell}\).

Choose a smooth coordinate chart \(u:U\to u(U)\subseteq\mathbb R^s\) of this cell about \(\Sigma_0\).  If \(s>0\), choose \(\rho>0\) with \(\overline B(u(\Sigma_0),\rho)\subset u(U)\), and define
\[
 \mathcal K_G
 =u^{-1}\!\left(\overline B(u(\Sigma_0),\rho)\right).        \tag{27}
\]
If \(s=0\), set \(\mathcal K_G=\{\Sigma_0\}\).  In both cases \(\mathcal K_G\) is nonempty and compact and has nonempty relative interior in \(\mathcal C_{G,e}\), as required by \(\mathrm{def:regular\mbox{-}class}\).

Finally, fix \(\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G\).  Since \(\Sigma\in\mathcal M_G\), its definition supplies real supported \(\Lambda\) and \(\Omega\succ0\) satisfying (23).  Multiplying by \((I_n-\Lambda)^{\mathsf T}\) and \(I_n-\Lambda\) gives
\[
 \Omega=(I_n-\Lambda)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(I_n-\Lambda).       \tag{28}
\]
For every missing bidirected pair, expansion of (28) gives \(F_{ij}(\Lambda,\Sigma)=\Omega_{ij}=0\).  Hence the real value \(\lambda_e\) has a complete real supported extension, and by definition
\[
 \lambda_e\in\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma).                         \tag{29}
\]
Thus \(\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma)\ne\varnothing\) throughout \(\mathcal K_G\).

Put \(d=d_e(G)\).  The finite minimal polynomial has \(d\geq1\), and on the successful output it specializes as
\[
 p_e(\Sigma,t)=t^d+\sum_{a=0}^{d-1}c_a(\Sigma)t^a.            \tag{30}
\]
Every \(c_a\) is a rational covariance circuit.  Since \(\mathcal K_G\subset\mathcal M_G\setminus\mathcal E_{G,e}\), all its denominator, specialized-leading-coefficient, and squarefreeness certificate factors are continuous and nonzero on \(\mathcal K_G\).  Compactness gives a positive minimum for the absolute value of each denominator, while the numerator circuits are bounded.  Therefore some \(M<\infty\) satisfies
\[
 \max_{0\leq a<d}|c_a(\Sigma)|\leq M
 \qquad\text{for every }\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G.              \tag{31}
\]

If \(z\) is a root of (30) and \(|z|>1+M\), then
\[
 |z|^d
 =\left|\sum_{a=0}^{d-1}c_a(\Sigma)z^a\right|
 \leq M\sum_{a=0}^{d-1}|z|^a
 =M\frac{|z|^d-1}{|z|-1}
 <|z|^d,                                                       \tag{32}
\]
a contradiction.  Thus all roots lie in the fixed disk \(|z|\leq1+M\).  The root-incidence set
\[
 \mathscr Z=\{(\Sigma,z)\in\mathcal K_G\times\mathbb C:
 p_e(\Sigma,z)=0\}                                           \tag{33}
\]
is closed in a compact set and hence compact.

The nonvanishing squarefreeness certificate says that \(p_e(\Sigma,\cdot)\) and \(\partial_t p_e(\Sigma,\cdot)\) have no common root on \(\mathcal K_G\).  Consequently \(\partial_t p_e\) is nonzero on (33), and continuity gives
\[
 \eta=\min_{(\Sigma,z)\in\mathscr Z}
 |\partial_t p_e(\Sigma,z)|>0.                               \tag{34}
\]

Suppose no uniform separation constant existed.  Then there would be \(\Sigma_\nu\in\mathcal K_G\) and distinct roots \(z_\nu,w_\nu\) of \(p_e(\Sigma_\nu,\cdot)\) with \(|z_\nu-w_\nu|\to0\).  Passing to a subsequence using compactness and (32),
\[
 \Sigma_\nu\to\Sigma_*,\qquad z_\nu\to z_*,\qquad
 w_\nu\to z_*.
\]
The divided difference
\[
 \mathfrak q(\Sigma,z,w)
 =\frac{p_e(\Sigma,z)-p_e(\Sigma,w)}{z-w}
\]
for \(z\ne w\) extends polynomially to the diagonal with \(\mathfrak q(\Sigma,z,z)=\partial_t p_e(\Sigma,z)\).  Since \(\mathfrak q(\Sigma_\nu,z_\nu,w_\nu)=0\), passage to the limit gives
\[
 p_e(\Sigma_*,z_*)=0,
 \qquad \partial_t p_e(\Sigma_*,z_*)=0,                      \tag{35}
\]
contradicting (34).  Thus some \(\gamma>0\) separates every pair of distinct complex roots uniformly on \(\mathcal K_G\).  Exceptional-set validity and real-root lifting make every retained real value one of these complex roots, so the same \(\gamma\) separates distinct retained roots.

Let \(q=n(n+1)/2\), fix an ordering \(\operatorname{vech}\) of symmetric entries, and define
\[
 W_r=\operatorname{vech}\!\left(
 X^{(r)}X^{(r)\mathsf T}-\Sigma\right).
\]
Then
\[
 \sqrt m\,\operatorname{vech}(S_m-\Sigma)
 =m^{-1/2}\sum_{r=1}^m W_r.                                  \tag{36}
\]
The independent Gaussian sampling assumption gives \(\mathbb E_\Sigma W_r=0\).  Differentiating the Gaussian moment-generating function four times gives
\[
 \mathbb E_\Sigma(X_iX_jX_kX_l)
 =\sigma_{ij}\sigma_{kl}+\sigma_{ik}\sigma_{jl}
  +\sigma_{il}\sigma_{jk},
\]
and hence
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}_\Sigma(W_{r,ij},W_{r,kl})
 =\sigma_{ik}\sigma_{jl}+\sigma_{il}\sigma_{jk}
 =(V_\Sigma)_{ij,kl}.                                        \tag{37}
\]

Compactness of \(\mathcal K_G\) bounds all fixed-order Gaussian moments uniformly; in particular, \(\sup_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}\mathbb E_\Sigma\|W_r\|^3<\infty\).  Taylor's formula for \(e^{ix}\) gives, for each fixed \(u\in\mathbb R^q\), uniformly over \(\mathcal K_G\),
\[
 \mathbb E_\Sigma\exp\!\left(
 \frac{i u^{\mathsf T}W_r}{\sqrt m}\right)
 =1-\frac{u^{\mathsf T}V_\Sigma u}{2m}+O(m^{-3/2}).          \tag{38}
\]
Taking the \(m\)-th power proves convergence of the characteristic function in (36) to \(\exp(-u^{\mathsf T}V_\Sigma u/2)\), uniformly in \(\Sigma\).  This is uniform weak convergence: the uniformly bounded second moments make every parameter sequence tight; from any \(m_\nu\to\infty\) and \(\Sigma_\nu\in\mathcal K_G\), compactness gives a subsequence with \(\Sigma_\nu\to\Sigma_*\), and (38) forces every weak subsequential limit to have the Gaussian characteristic function with covariance \(V_{\Sigma_*}\).  Uniqueness follows, for example, by convolution with \(N(0,\varepsilon I_q)\), Fourier inversion, and then \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).  Thus
\[
 \sqrt m\,\operatorname{vech}(S_m-\Sigma)
 \rightsquigarrow N(0,V_\Sigma)                              \tag{39}
\]
uniformly on \(\mathcal K_G\).  The same second-moment bound and Markov's inequality give
\[
 \|S_m-\Sigma\|=O_{\mathbb P}(m^{-1/2})                     \tag{40}
\]
uniformly.

Write \(\widehat\Sigma_m=\pi_G(S_m)\) on the projection tube.  Since \(\pi_G(\Sigma)=\Sigma\) on \(\mathcal K_G\), smoothness on a neighborhood and compactness yield the uniform expansion
\[
 \operatorname{vech}(\widehat\Sigma_m-\Sigma)
 =D\pi_G(\Sigma)\operatorname{vech}(S_m-\Sigma)
  +O_{\mathbb P}(\|S_m-\Sigma\|^2).                          \tag{41}
\]
Every coefficient circuit of \(p_e\) is smooth near \(\mathcal K_G\), because its finitely many denominators are bounded away from zero.  The derived root-separation lemma gives both a common separation margin and, through its compact root-incidence argument, a positive lower bound for \(|\partial_t p_e|\) at every root.  Taylor expansion of \(p_e(\Theta,t)=0\), with this linear coefficient bounded away from zero and second derivatives uniformly bounded, produces a unique smooth local branch through every retained root.  Implicit differentiation gives
\[
 Dr_j(\Sigma)[H]
 =-\frac{D_\Sigma p_e(\Sigma,r_j(\Sigma))[H]}
          {\partial_t p_e(\Sigma,r_j(\Sigma))}.              \tag{42}
\]
Increasing order, the separation margin \(\gamma\), and constancy of the real-extension labels on the connected regular cell give a common labeling \(r=(r_1,\ldots,r_J)\).  A finite cover of \(\mathcal K_G\) by these root neighborhoods makes the first two branch derivatives uniformly bounded.  Combining (39)--(42) yields
\[
 \sqrt m\{r(\pi_G(S_m))-r(\Sigma)\}
 \rightsquigarrow N\!\left(0,
 Dr(\Sigma)D\pi_G(\Sigma)V_\Sigma
 D\pi_G(\Sigma)^{\mathsf T}Dr(\Sigma)^{\mathsf T}\right)  \tag{43}
\]
uniformly on \(\mathcal K_G\).

All certificate factors are continuous and nonzero on \(\mathcal K_G\), and all root-extension labels are locally constant along the selected stratum.  Compactness supplies a relative neighborhood \(U\) of \(\mathcal K_G\) on which the projection is defined, every certificate remains valid, and the same \(J\) branches are retained.  Define
\[
 \mathcal H_m=\left\{
 \begin{array}{l}
 S_m\text{ lies in the projection tube},\quad
 \widehat\Sigma_m\in U,\\[2pt]
 \displaystyle\max_{1\leq j\leq J}
 |r_j(\widehat\Sigma_m)-r_j(\Sigma)|<\gamma/3
 \end{array}\right\}.                                      \tag{44}
\]
Uniform consistency in (40)--(41), uniform continuity of the root maps, and the positive certificate and separation margins imply
\[
 \inf_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}\Pr_\Sigma(\mathcal H_m)  o1. \tag{45}
\]
On \(\mathcal H_m\), real-root lifting and the estimator definition give
\[
 \widehat{\mathcal R}_{e,m}
 =\{r_1(\widehat\Sigma_m),\ldots,r_J(\widehat\Sigma_m)\}.   \tag{46}
\]
The separation in (44) makes this a bijective matching to \(\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma)\), and regular-cell existence gives \(J\geq1\), so the set in (46) is nonempty.  Moreover,
\[
 d_H\!\left(\widehat{\mathcal R}_{e,m},
              \mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma)\right)
 \leq\max_{1\leq j\leq J}
 |r_j(\widehat\Sigma_m)-r_j(\Sigma)|
 =O_{\mathbb P}(m^{-1/2})                                    \tag{47}
\]
uniformly by (43).  Although the defined Hausdorff distance may be infinite on \(\mathcal H_m^c\), (45) makes that event uniformly negligible, which is exactly enough for the uniform \(O_{\mathbb P}\) assertion.  Also,
\[
 \sup_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}
 \Pr_\Sigma(\widehat{\mathcal R}_{e,m}=\varnothing)
 \leq\sup_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}\Pr_\Sigma(\mathcal H_m^c)
 \to0.                                                        \tag{48}
\]

For simultaneous neighborhoods, let \(s=\dim\mathcal C_{G,e}\) and put
\[
 W_\pi(\Sigma)=D\pi_G(\Sigma)V_\Sigma D\pi_G(\Sigma)^{\mathsf T}. \tag{49}
\]
The ambient covariance matrix \(V_\Sigma\) is positive definite on symmetric-coordinate directions: for a nonzero symmetric matrix \(H\), (37) gives
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_\Sigma(X^{\mathsf T}HX)
 =2\operatorname{tr}\!\left(
   (\Sigma^{1/2}H\Sigma^{1/2})^2\right)>0.                   \tag{50}
\]
Because \(\pi_G\) fixes the smooth stratum, its derivative is the identity on the tangent space and has that \(s\)-dimensional space as its image.  Thus \(W_\pi\) has rank \(s\).  Compactness bounds its smallest positive eigenvalue away from zero, so its Moore--Penrose inverse varies continuously.  With \(\widehat W_{\pi,m}\) the plug-in version at \(\widehat\Sigma_m\), (39)--(41) and continuous diagonalization on this fixed-rank image give
\[
 m\,\operatorname{vech}(\widehat\Sigma_m-\Sigma)^{\mathsf T}
 \widehat W_{\pi,m}^{+}
 \operatorname{vech}(\widehat\Sigma_m-\Sigma)
 \rightsquigarrow\chi_s^2                                  \tag{51}
\]
uniformly.  Indeed, for \(Z\sim N(0,W_\pi)\), the quadratic form \(Z^{\mathsf T}W_\pi^+Z\) is the sum of \(s\) independent squared standard normals.

Let \(E_m\) be the corresponding joint covariance ellipsoid in the regular projected neighborhood, with the \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile of \(\chi_s^2\).  Equation (51) gives
\[
 \liminf_{m\to\infty}\inf_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}
 \Pr_\Sigma(\Sigma\in E_m)\geq1-\alpha.                    \tag{52}
\]
For \(s=0\), take the degenerate ellipsoid on the locally constant projected point, for which the limiting coverage is one.  As prescribed in \(\mathrm{def:branch\mbox{-}neighborhoods}\), set
\[
 \mathcal A_{m,j}=r_j(E_m),\qquad 1\leq j\leq J.             \tag{53}
\]
Whenever \(\Sigma\in E_m\), all inclusions \(r_j(\Sigma)\in\mathcal A_{m,j}\) hold simultaneously.  Therefore
\[
 \liminf_{m\to\infty}\inf_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}
 \Pr_\Sigma\!\left(
 r_j(\Sigma)\in\mathcal A_{m,j}\text{ for every }1\leq j\leq J
 \right)\geq1-\alpha.                                       \tag{54}
\]
This construction covers all retained branches and makes no branch selection.

Assume \(\mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma)=\{r_1(\Sigma)\}\) throughout \(\mathcal K_G\).  On the events \(\mathcal H_m\) supplied by \(\mathrm{thm:regular\mbox{-}finite\mbox{-}set\mbox{-}inference}\), the estimated set is bijectively matched to this singleton.  Hence it has exactly one element, denoted \(\widehat r_m\), and
\[
 \inf_{\Sigma\in\mathcal K_G}\Pr_\Sigma\!\left(
 \widehat{\mathcal R}_{e,m}=\{\widehat r_m\}\right)\to1.   \tag{55}
\]
Define \(\widehat r_m=0\) outside the singleton event.  By (55), this extension changes the statistic only on an event of probability tending to zero uniformly.

For singleton sets the Hausdorff distance equals absolute error.  The finite-set inference theorem therefore yields
\[
 |\widehat r_m-r_1(\Sigma)|
 =d_H\!\left(\widehat{\mathcal R}_{e,m},
              \mathcal R_e(G,\Sigma)\right)
 =O_{\mathbb P}(m^{-1/2})                                    \tag{56}
\]
uniformly on \(\mathcal K_G\), after using (55) to discard the negligible complement.  This proves consistency.

Taking the first coordinate of the joint branch limit in that theorem gives
\[
 \sqrt m\{\widehat r_m-r_1(\Sigma)\}
 \rightsquigarrow N(0,W_{11}(\Sigma)),                        \tag{57}
\]
where
\[
 W(\Sigma)=Dr(\Sigma)D\pi_G(\Sigma)V_\Sigma
 D\pi_G(\Sigma)^{\mathsf T}Dr(\Sigma)^{\mathsf T}.          \tag{58}
\]
The uniformly negligible modification outside \(\mathcal H_m\) does not affect (57).  Its variance is precisely the corresponding diagonal entry asserted in the proposition; if that entry is zero, (57) denotes the degenerate centered normal law, so no unstated nondegeneracy condition is required.

Fix one source-consistent recorded stratum and use the notation of \(\mathrm{def:source\mbox{-}prime\mbox{-}chart}\).  Thus \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_r)\), \(r\leq 2k\), \(P=\ker\xi\subset K_G[x]\), and validity of the supplied chart gives
\[
 P K_G[x]_{H\Delta}=(h_1,\ldots,h_c)K_G[x]_{H\Delta},
 \qquad \xi(H\Delta)\neq0,                                   \tag{1}
\]
where \(c=\operatorname{ht}P\), the sequence \(h_1,\ldots,h_c\) is reduced and regular after localization, and \(\Delta\) is a nonzero \(c\)-by-\(c\) Jacobian minor.  Hence (1) defines the localization of the source prime itself, rather than an extensional union of residual components.  The Jacobian minor and regular-sequence hypotheses give a smooth, pure-dimensional principal open subset of dimension
\[
 q=r-c\leq 2k.                                                \tag{2}
\]
The inequation \(H\Delta\neq0\) can be encoded without changing that subset by adjoining a variable \(u\) and the equation \(uH\Delta-1=0\).

Put \(E=K_G(\lambda_e)\).  Since \(d_e(G)<\infty\), \(E/K_G\) is finite; since the characteristic is zero, it is separable.  Its \(d_e(G)\) embeddings into \(\overline{K_G}\) give the distinct conjugates of \(\lambda_e\).  For each embedding \(\tau:E\to\overline{K_G}\), the tensor product \(L\otimes_{E,\tau}\overline{K_G}\) is nonzero: choosing an \(E\)-transcendence basis of \(L\) reduces this assertion to tensoring a finite field extension with an algebraic closure.  The corresponding affine model therefore has a nonempty conjugate component.  Moreover, \(H\Delta\), which is nonzero at the source generic point, remains nonzero on that component.  Generic affine hyperplanes meet each positive-dimensional component properly.  Because there are only finitely many conjugate components, the intersection of the corresponding nonempty open sets of hyperplane choices is nonempty.  Consequently one may choose \(q\) affine linear forms whose successive intersections are transverse, zero-dimensional, and nonempty on every conjugate component.  Equivalently, this is the generic transverse slicing operation covered by \(\mathrm{lem:groebner\mbox{-}free\mbox{-}geometric\mbox{-}resolution}\).  Random choices outside the finitely many associated determinant and leading-form hypersurfaces have this property.

Apply that cited geometric-resolution lemma to the localized regular sequence together with the \(q\) slices.  On a successful choice it returns a finite reduced \(K_G\)-algebra \(B_{mathfrak C}\), multiplication matrices for the exposed coordinates, and a primitive-element representation.  The lifting circuits in the valid chart recover every eliminated directed coordinate, including \(\lambda_e\), and their substitution into every original residual is zero in the localized source-prime algebra.  Let \(M_{e,mathfrak C}\) denote multiplication by the recovered \(\lambda_e\) on \(B_{mathfrak C}\), and set
\[
 \chi_{e,mathfrak C}(t)=\det(tI-M_{e,mathfrak C}).           \tag{3}
\]
Every geometric point represented by (3) lies on a base change of the source prime, so its queried coordinate is a conjugate of \(\lambda_e\).  Conversely, the common slicing choice meets every conjugate component, so every conjugate occurs as an eigenvalue in at least one chart.  Taking the squarefree part of the product of the polynomials (3) over all source-consistent recorded strata therefore gives a monic polynomial with exactly the distinct conjugates of \(\lambda_e\) as its roots.  Uniqueness of the monic polynomial with those roots yields
\[
 p_e(t)=\operatorname{sqfree}\!\left(
       \prod_{mathfrak C}\chi_{e,mathfrak C}(t)\right),
 \qquad \deg p_e=d_e(G).                                    \tag{4}
\]
Thus (4) reports the single-coordinate degree, independently of the cardinality or dimension of the unsliced full parameter fiber.  The orientation upper-bound theorem additionally gives
\[
 \deg p_e=d_e(G)
 \leq 2^{\min\{|D|-n+2,\binom{n-2}{2}\}},                  \tag{5}
\]
but no use of whole-fiber degree is made.

All chart coefficients, multiplication matrices, and lifting maps are elements of \(K_G\) represented by rational arithmetic circuits in the covariance entries.  Determinants, polynomial differentiation, subresultant greatest-common-divisor computation, squarefree extraction, and monic normalization are arithmetic-circuit operations over \(K_G\); hence (4) gives coefficientwise rational circuits for \(p_e\).  Equality (1) prevents a factor belonging only to a different residual component from entering (4).  For every rational lifting identity, clearing denominators produces both a pole factor and an incidence-lifting identity.  Homogenization before slicing produces the projective leading-form factors; the univariate output produces its specialized leading-coefficient and squarefreeness-resultant factors.  The covariance denominators are recorded separately.  Finally, applying \(\mathrm{lem:effective\mbox{-}real\mbox{-}quantifier\mbox{-}elimination}\) to the original supported residual equations and \(\mathrm{lem:real\mbox{-}algebraic\mbox{-}sampling}\) after exact specialization supplies the real-lifting sign and sample-point circuits.  These finitely many circuits form \(\mathcal Q_{G,e}\); after clearing covariance denominators and deleting repetitions, their nonzero product is \(h_{G,e}\).  By \(\mathrm{thm:incidence\mbox{-}localization}\), this bookkeeping inverts no directed-coordinate expression and so does not discard a pole or an identically zero-over-zero stratum.

It remains to establish the resource and error bounds.  The arbitrary-equation and inequation operations on recorded strata are covered by \(\mathrm{lem:lifting\mbox{-}fiber\mbox{-}equidimensional\mbox{-}decomposition}\), while the regular slices are covered by \(\mathrm{lem:groebner\mbox{-}free\mbox{-}geometric\mbox{-}resolution}\).  Their complexity bounds, multiplication-matrix linear algebra, and (2) imply that for a universal \(a>0\) the total number of arithmetic operations and output gates is at most
\[
 (n+s)^{a(k+1)}\mathfrak d^{,a}
 \operatorname{poly}(\log(1/\delta)),                        \tag{6}
\]
where \(s=s(\mathfrak C_{G,e})\) and \(\mathfrak d=\mathfrak d(\mathfrak C_{G,e})\).  Every randomized genericity decision is the nonvanishing test of an explicitly constructed chart, transversality, leading-form, lifting, or resultant polynomial.  If their degree bounds are \(d_1,\ldots,d_N\), choose the independently sampled finite-field sets so that each allocated error is at most \(\delta/N\).  The Schwartz--Zippel bound and the union bound then give
\[
 \Pr(\text{some symbolic genericity decision is wrong})
 \leq\sum_{j=1}^N \frac{d_j}{|S_j|}\leq\delta.              \tag{7}
\]
On the complementary event, (1)--(4) show that the returned tuple is exactly \((d_e(G),p_e,\mathcal Q_{G,e},h_{G,e})\).

If \(s\leq n^b\) and \(\mathfrak d\leq n^{b(k+1)}\), then, after enlarging a constant to cover \(n\geq2\),
\[
 (n+s)^{a(k+1)}\mathfrak d^{,a}
 \leq n^{a(\max\{1,b\}+1+b)(k+1)}
 \leq n^{C(k+1)}.                                            \tag{8}
\]
This proves the stated fixed-parameter specialization of (6).

The antecedent is essential to what has been proved: the two cited geometric algorithms solve or decompose equations once the localized reduced chart has been supplied, but neither identifies the embedded source-prime component nor constructs a source-nonzero Jacobian minor with bounded rational circuits over \(K_G\).  The argument therefore constructs and certifies the claimed output exactly under, and only under, the supplied-valid-chart hypothesis.
